title: Suicide in Children
summary: What suicide is, why people attempt it, how it affects children, the warning signs that often come first, and how treatment and prevention work.

lesson.title: Hearing the cry before it is too late
lesson.hook: We like to think of childhood as carefree. That is exactly why a child's suicidal thoughts are so often missed. The signs are usually there; adults just are not expecting them.

slides.heading: Defining suicide
slides.body:
**Edwin Shneidman** defined suicide as an **intentioned death**: a **direct, conscious and deliberate** effort to end one's own life.

Suicide is often described as the **most disastrous consequence of depression**. Your course notes it is common among young people and a leading cause of death among college students. Most people facing hardship **never** attempt suicide, which is why researchers ask what makes some people more vulnerable.

left.title: Surcease
points: Desire to end it all
Escape from unbearable pain
Seeing no other way out

right.title: Manipulation
points: Desire to change the world or other people
The attempt as a message
A cry to be heard

steps.title: Alcohol and drug use
steps.detail: Lowers inhibitions and deepens low mood.

steps.title: Modelling
steps.detail: Exposure to suicide by others, including in the media.

slides.question: The two fundamental motivations for suicide are:
slides.why: Surcease is the wish to end it all; manipulation is the wish to change others or the world through the act.

slides.heading: Theories and their limits
slides.body:
The leading explanations come from **psychodynamic**, **socio-cultural** and **biological** perspectives. Each has some support, but research backing is **limited**, and none explains the **full range** of suicidal acts.

Risk also **changes across the lifespan**, so children deserve focused attention of their own.

slides.heading: Children and suicide
slides.body:
Suicide in children is **infrequent**, but it has been **increasing** over recent decades. US figures in the course cite about **500 children under 14** dying by suicide each year, with **boys outnumbering girls** by as much as **5 to 1**.

About **1 in 100** children is estimated to try to harm themselves. One study found many child attempters had **attempted before**, and **half** lived with **only one parent**.

terms.meaning: Repeated running away or unusual numbers of 'accidents'
Acting out, explosive anger, giving up easily
Calling oneself useless, stupid or a burden
Loneliness, isolation, extreme sensitivity to criticism
Dark fantasies, marked personality change, strong interest in death

slides.heading: A letter home
slides.story: A ten-year-old boy left a note telling his parents he loved them, that he could not cope with school any more, and that he wanted to die, ending with 'Help me'. Reported by Pfeiffer (1986), the letter shows both motivations at once: wanting the pain to end, and desperately asking to be rescued.
slides.takeaway: Children's suicidal messages often mix despair with a plea for help; every such message must be taken seriously.

slides.question: Which of the following is a recognised warning sign of suicide risk in a child?
options: Marked personality change and preoccupation with death
slides.why: Personality change and preoccupation with death are important warning signs.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'define suicide' (Shneidman), 'list the two motivations' (surcease, manipulation) and 'mention five behavioural patterns that precede suicide attempts'. Note the 5 to 1 boy-girl ratio for completed child suicides. Trap: treating childhood suicidal talk as attention-seeking to be ignored. Always respond seriously.
slides.sampleQuestion: Mention five behavioural patterns that commonly precede suicide attempts by young people.
slides.howToAnswer: Any five of: running away, accident-proneness, temper tantrums, self-depreciation, withdrawal and loneliness, extreme sensitivity to criticism, low frustration tolerance, dark fantasies, marked personality change, preoccupation with death.

points: Suicide: intentional, direct, conscious effort to end one's life (Shneidman).
Motivations: surcease (end it all) and manipulation (change others).
Triggers: stress, mood and thought changes, drugs, mental disorder, modelling.
Child suicide is rare but rising; boys outnumber girls up to 5 to 1.
Warning signs include withdrawal, self-depreciation and death preoccupation.

questions.stem: Edwin Shneidman defined suicide as:
options: An intentioned death involving a direct, conscious effort to end one's life
questions.explanation: Shneidman stressed intention, directness and consciousness.

questions.stem: Suicide is often described as the most disastrous consequence of:
questions.explanation: Depression is strongly linked to suicide.

questions.stem: 'Surcease' as a motivation for suicide means:
questions.explanation: Surcease is the wish to end suffering by ending life.

questions.stem: Among children who die by suicide, boys outnumber girls by as much as:
questions.explanation: The course cites ratios up to 5 to 1.

questions.stem: 'Manipulation' as a motivation refers to:
options: Wanting to change the world or other people through the attempt
questions.explanation: Manipulation uses the act to affect others.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a recognised trigger for suicidal acts?
questions.explanation: Exposure to others' suicide can trigger suicidal acts.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old who used to be cheerful becomes withdrawn, gives away her favourite things and keeps talking about death. The best response is to:
options: Take it seriously, talk with her and get professional help
questions.explanation: These are warning signs; prompt, caring action and professional help are needed.

questions.stem: A boy constantly calls himself 'useless' and 'a burden'. This warning sign is:
questions.explanation: Putting oneself down persistently is self-depreciation.

questions.stem: A teenager makes a suicide attempt partly hoping her divorcing parents will reunite. This reflects which motivation?
questions.explanation: Seeking to change others' behaviour reflects manipulation.

questions.stem: All of the following commonly precede suicide attempts by young people EXCEPT:
options: Sudden increase in long-term goal planning with friends
questions.explanation: Future-oriented planning with friends is not a listed warning sign.

questions.stem: Which statement about theories of suicide is correct?
options: One theory fully explains all suicides
Psychodynamic, socio-cultural and biological theories have limited support and miss the full range of acts
questions.explanation: Each perspective explains part of the picture but none is complete.

questions.stem: One study of child suicide attempters found that half were:
questions.explanation: Half lived with one parent; a quarter had attempted before.

questions.stem: I. Suicide in children has been increasing over recent decades. II. Most people facing difficulty attempt suicide. III. Previous attempts raise future risk. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. Most people facing hardship never attempt suicide.

questions.stem: Why is childhood suicide often overlooked?
options: Adults assume childhood is carefree and miss warning signs
questions.explanation: Beliefs about a happy childhood make adults less alert to warning signs.

questions.stem: A child's note expresses both a wish to die and the words 'Help me'. This shows that:
options: The child is only seeking attention
Suicidal communication can combine despair with a genuine plea for rescue
questions.explanation: Surcease and manipulation can coexist; such messages demand serious response.

lesson.title: Responding and preventing
lesson.hook: In 1953, a London vicar began answering phone calls from people in despair. That simple idea, someone to talk to at the worst moment, grew into one of the world's largest suicide prevention networks.

slides.heading: Contributing conditions
slides.body: Child suicide has been linked to the **recent or expected loss** of a loved one and to **family stress**. Wider conditions such as **poverty** and parental **unemployment** can lead to depression that eventually contributes to suicide attempts.

slides.heading: Do children understand death?
slides.body:
Many people assume young children cannot fully grasp death, placing them in Shneidman's category of '**death ignorers**', who believe they will continue to exist, like a boy who hoped to **join his mother in heaven**.

Yet many child suicides seem to rest on a **clear understanding** of death and a real **wish to die**. Interviews with schoolchildren found **6 to 33%** had **thought about suicide** (Culp et al., 1995).

terms.meaning: Clearly intend to end their lives at the time they act
Believe they are already dying and hasten the process
Believe death will not end their existence
Feel mixed about dying and take risks that may or may not end their life

slides.question: A child who believes he will go to heaven and still be with his mother after death fits which of Shneidman's categories?
slides.why: Death ignorers believe their existence will continue after death.

left.title: After an attempt
points: Medical care for injuries
Psychotherapy, inpatient or outpatient
Support for family and friends

right.title: Prevention
points: Crisis intervention
Long-term therapy
Public education and safer environments

slides.heading: Suicide prevention programmes
slides.body:
The first prevention programme in **England**, the **Samaritans**, began in **1953**; the first in the **United States** was founded in **Los Angeles** (your course gives 1955). Today, many **mental health centres, hospital emergency units and pastoral counselling centres** include prevention services.

They offer **crisis intervention**: helping people see their situation more **accurately**, make **better decisions**, act **constructively** and get through the crisis, followed by **longer-term therapy**.

slides.heading: Wider prevention
slides.body:
Prevention also means **reducing access to common means** of suicide, through measures such as **firearm control**, **safer medication packaging** and **storage**.

Many experts see **public education** as the ultimate form of prevention: teaching parents, teachers and young people the warning signs and how to respond. If you or someone you know is struggling, talk to a trusted adult, your university counselling unit or a doctor.

slides.heading: The school that listened
slides.story: After a pupil's death shook a secondary school in Enugu, staff trained all teachers to recognise warning signs and set up a confidential counsellor's room. Months later, a teacher noticed a JSS3 girl withdrawing and writing about death. A gentle conversation led to counselling and family support. She is now in SS2, doing well.
slides.takeaway: Education and early, caring intervention can prevent child suicide.

slides.question: Crisis intervention in suicide prevention aims mainly to:
options: Help the person see their situation more accurately and get through the crisis
slides.why: Crisis intervention offers immediate support to clarify thinking and survive the crisis, then links to longer therapy.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'state the two categories of suicide treatment' (after an attempt, and prevention) and questions on the Samaritans (1953), crisis intervention and public education. Know Shneidman's 'death ignorer' and the 6 to 33% figure. Trap: assuming children cannot understand death; many do.
slides.sampleQuestion: State and explain the two major categories of treatment for suicidal people.
slides.howToAnswer: Treatment after an attempt: medical care, then inpatient or outpatient therapy, with support for family. Prevention: crisis intervention, long-term therapy, restricting means and public education.

points: Loss, family stress, poverty and unemployment contribute to child suicide.
Some children are 'death ignorers'; many understand death clearly.
6 to 33% of schoolchildren report suicidal thoughts.
Treatment: care after an attempt, and prevention.
Prevention: crisis intervention, therapy, restricting means, public education.

questions.stem: The two major categories of suicide treatment are:
options: Treatment after an attempt and suicide prevention
questions.explanation: Treatment divides into care after attempts and prevention.

questions.stem: The first suicide prevention programme in England was called:
questions.explanation: The Samaritans started in 1953.

questions.stem: Shneidman's 'death ignorers' believe that:
options: Death will not end their existence
questions.explanation: Death ignorers expect to continue existing after death.

questions.stem: Interviews with schoolchildren found that what percentage had thought about suicide?
questions.explanation: Culp and colleagues (1995) found 6 to 33%.

questions.stem: Crisis intervention is a key service of:
questions.explanation: Prevention programmes offer crisis intervention.

questions.stem: Which measure reduces access to common means of suicide?
options: Safer medication packaging and firearm control
questions.explanation: Restricting access to means is a proven prevention approach.

questions.stem: A boy says he wants to die so he can be with his late grandmother in heaven. Shneidman would classify him as a:
questions.explanation: Believing existence continues after death marks a death ignorer.

questions.stem: After a teenager survives an attempt, she receives medical care and then weekly therapy, while her parents get support. This is:
questions.explanation: Medical and psychological care after an attempt falls in the first category.

questions.stem: A state trains all teachers to recognise suicide warning signs. Many experts see this kind of public education as:
questions.explanation: Public education is often called the ultimate prevention.

questions.stem: Which statement about children's understanding of death is MOST accurate?
options: All children see death as temporary
Some children are death ignorers, but many child suicides reflect a clear understanding of death
questions.explanation: Both patterns exist; many children do understand death.

questions.stem: Why is long-term therapy needed after crisis intervention?
options: The underlying problems that led to the crisis still need treatment
questions.explanation: Crisis help gets people through the moment; therapy addresses root causes.

questions.stem: All of the following can contribute to child suicide EXCEPT:
options: Recent loss of a loved one
questions.explanation: Supportive relationships protect against suicide.

questions.stem: I. Crisis intervention helps people see their situation more accurately. II. Treatment can also benefit relatives and friends. III. Restricting access to means plays no role in prevention. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and II are correct. Restricting access to means is an important prevention strategy.

questions.stem: A classmate tells you she has been thinking about ending her life. The most helpful first response is to:
options: Listen calmly, take it seriously and help her reach a counsellor or trusted adult
questions.explanation: Taking it seriously and connecting her with help is the right first step.

questions.stem: Which pairing of person and contribution is correct?
options: Shneidman: defined suicide as intentioned death
questions.explanation: Shneidman defined suicide and described death ignorers; Culp and colleagues surveyed schoolchildren.
